1.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [he remains faithful to his covenant]

The psalmist is using **to forever** as a common expression of his culture to mean “eternally” or “for all time.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [everlasting]

2.note: The expression **the redeemed of Yahweh** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is Yahweh. Alternate translation: [those whom Yahweh has redeemed]

By using **Let**, the psalmist is expressing what he desires or prays will happen. See the discussion in the introduction to this book about “let” and “may” and follow the decision of your team of how a speaker will express in this context what he wants someone to do. Alternate translation: [I desire that the redeemed of Yahweh say that they have been redeemed]

It might seem that the expression **who he rescued them** contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [whom he rescued]

Here, **hand** represents the power or control of a person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from the control of the opponent]

The psalmist is not referring to a specific **opponent**. He means opponents in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [every opponent]

3.note: The psalmist is referring to all of the earth by naming two extremes, **the sunrise** (the east) and **the evening** (the west), **the north** and **the sea** (the south). If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [from all directions and from everywhere in between]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [he has gathered them from the sunrise and from the evening, from the north and from the sea]

The psalmist assumes that readers will know that **the sunrise and the evening** refer to the east and the west. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [from the east and from the west]

The implication is that **the sea** refers to the southern sea, since the psalmist has already mentioned the other three directions (east, west, and north). You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [from the north and from the south]

4.note: The pronoun **They** refers to the redeemed people whom Yahweh has gathered from foreign lands, as mentioned in the previous verses. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Some of them wandered]

By **with wilderness for a road**, the psalmist means that they had no proper road to travel on, only the trackless wilderness. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [with no road to walk on, only wilderness]

5.note: The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language as modeled in the UST.

David is using **their soul fainted within them** as a common expression of his culture to mean “they felt like they were dying” or “they became weak and discouraged.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they felt like they were dying]

6.note: The psalmist is using the adjective **distressing** as a noun to mean a certain kind of situation. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [in their distress]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **distresses**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [from the distressing things that were happening to them]

7.note: The psalmist is using the possessive form to describe **a city** that is characterized by **dwelling**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [a city to dwell in]

8.note: Here and repeatedly throughout this psalm, the psalmist is using **May** to express his wish or desire that the people would praise Yahweh. See the discussion in the introduction to this book about “let” and “may” and follow the decision of your team of how a speaker will express in this context what he wants someone to do. Alternate translation: [I desire that they thank Yahweh]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [for being faithful to his covenant]

The psalmist is using **sons of man** as a common expression of his culture to mean “people” or “humanity.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [for mankind]

9.note: The psalmist is not referring to a specific **thirsty soul**. He means thirsty people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [every thirsty soul]

The psalmist is using the term **soul** to mean the entire person from the perspective of his spiritual and emotional existence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [any thirsty person]

The psalmist is not referring to a specific **hungry soul**. He means hungry souls in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and every hungry soul]
Here, **soul** represents the entire person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and any hungry person]

The psalmist is using the adjective **good** as a noun to mean good things. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [he fills with good things]

10.note: The word **Sitting** starts a new section of the psalm and refers to another thing that happened to some of Yahweh’s people. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Some of Yahweh’s people had to sit in]

The terms **darkness** and **gloom** mean similar things. The psalmist is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [depressing darkness]

The psalmist is using the possessive form to describe **prisoners** that are characterized by **affliction and iron**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [prisoners afflicted by iron fetters]

The phrase **affliction and iron** expresses a single idea. The word **affliction** tells more about **iron**. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [prisoners held by painful iron chains]

11.note: These two phrases **had rebelled against the words of God** and **despised the counsel of the Most High** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [they had rebelled against the words of God, indeed, they had despised the counsel of the Most High]

Here, **words** represents what God said by using words. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they had rebelled against God when he instructed them]

12.note: Here, **their hearts** represents their inner selves or their pride. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [them]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **hardship**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [by making them suffer]

Here the psalmist is speaking of the prisoners experiencing difficulties and hardships as if they **stumbled** while walking. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they experienced troubles]

13.q: וַ⁠יִּזְעֲק֣וּ אֶל־יְ֭הוָה בַּ⁠צַּ֣ר לָ⁠הֶ֑ם מִ֝⁠מְּצֻֽקוֹתֵי⁠הֶ֗ם יוֹשִׁיעֵֽ⁠ם
13.note: See how you translated the similar phrases in Psalms 107:6. Alternate translation: [Then they prayed to Yahweh to help them in their trouble and he saved them from it]

The psalmist is using the adjective **distressing** as a noun to mean a certain kind of situation. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [in their distress]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **distresses**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [from the distressing things that were happening to them]

14.note: The terms **darkness** and **gloom** mean similar things. The psalmist is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [of deep darkness]
If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the part about breaking **their bonds** before the part about bringing **them out of the darkness**, as in the UST.

15.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [for being faithful to his covenant]

The psalmist is using **the sons of man** as a common expression of his culture to mean “people” or “human beings.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [for mankind]

16.q: כִּֽי־שִׁ֭בַּר דַּלְת֣וֹת נְחֹ֑שֶׁת וּ⁠בְרִיחֵ֖י בַרְזֶ֣ל גִּדֵּֽעַ
16.note: If it is more natural in your language to state the reason before the result, you could do so by moving this sentence to the previous verse. You would then present the combined verses as 15–16 as modeled in the UST.

16.q: כִּֽי־שִׁ֭בַּר דַּלְת֣וֹת נְחֹ֑שֶׁת וּ⁠בְרִיחֵ֖י בַרְזֶ֣ל גִּדֵּֽעַ
16.note: The implication is that God freed the prisoners by breaking down the prison **gates** and **bars**. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [For he has freed them from prison by breaking down the gates of bronze and cutting through the bars of iron]

The word translated as **For** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [They should do this because]

The psalmist is using the possessive form to describe **gates** that are characterized by being made of **bronze**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the gates made of bronze]

The psalmist is using the possessive form to describe **bars** that are characterized by being made of **iron**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the bars made of iron]

17.note: The word **Foolish** starts a new section of the psalm and refers to another thing that happened to some of Yahweh’s people. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Some of Yahweh’s people became foolish]
The implication is that they were rebelling against Yahweh. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [because of rebelling against Yahweh]

18.note: The psalmist is using the term **their soul** to mean the entire person from the perspective of his spiritual/emotional existence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [they]

The psalmist is using **touched the gates of death** as a common expression of his culture to mean “came very close to dying.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and they came close to dying]

19.q: וַ⁠יִּזְעֲק֣וּ אֶל־יְ֭הוָה בַּ⁠צַּ֣ר לָ⁠הֶ֑ם מִ֝⁠מְּצֻֽקוֹתֵי⁠הֶ֗ם יוֹשִׁיעֵֽ⁠ם
19.note: See how you translated the similar phrases in Psalm 107:6 and Psalm 107:13. Alternate translation: [Then they prayed to Yahweh to help them in their trouble and he saved them from it]

The psalmist is using the adjective **distressing** as a noun to mean a certain kind of situation. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [in their distress]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **distresses**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [from the distressing things that were happening to them]

20.note: Here the psalmist is speaking of Yahweh’s healing power as if it were **his word** that he could send like a messenger. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he commanded that they be healed]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **destruction**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [from destroying themselves]

21.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [for being faithful to his covenant]

The psalmist is using **the sons of man** as a common expression of the culture to mean “mankind” or “all people.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [for mankind]

22.note: The psalmist is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [May they offer sacrifices of thanksgiving]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **thanksgiving**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [May they sacrifice sacrifices in order to thank him]

By **with a shout**, the psalmist means with a joyful shout or loud, celebratory exclamation. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [by shouting joyfully]

23.note: The words **Going down** start a new section of the psalm and refer to another thing that some of Yahweh’s people did. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Some of Yahweh’s people went down]

The implication is that the **abundant waters** are the open seas where merchants would travel for international trade. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [by crossing large amounts of water]

24.note: The psalmist is stating the pronoun **they** separately, even though the verb translated as **they saw** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that they are the only ones who saw the wonders that Yahweh created in the sea. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [they are the ones who saw]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **wonders**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and the wonderful things he did]

By **in the deep**, the psalmist means in the deep parts of the ocean. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [in the deep parts of the ocean]

25.note: Here, **Then he spoke and aroused** marks **the wind of a hurricane** as the goal or purpose of **he spoke**. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. Alternate translation: [Then he spoke to the wind so that it become as strong as a hurricane]

26.note: The psalmist says **They went up to the sky; they went down to the depths** as an extreme statement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [They went up very high; they went down very low]

By **They went up to the sky; they went down to the depths**, the psalmist means that the ships were lifted high on the waves and then dropped low into the troughs between the waves. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [The waves would carry their ships up to the sky; then the ships would fall to the depths between the waves]

Here the psalmist is speaking as if the sailors’ **souls melted** from fear and terror during the storm. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [They lost all courage in the disaster]

27.note: The psalmist is using the adjective **intoxicated** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [as though they were intoxicated]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **wisdom**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and even though they were wise about sailing, they did not know what to do]

28.q: וַ⁠יִּצְעֲק֣וּ אֶל־יְ֭הוָה בַּ⁠צַּ֣ר לָ⁠הֶ֑ם וּֽ֝⁠מִ⁠מְּצֽוּקֹתֵי⁠הֶ֗ם יוֹצִיאֵֽ⁠ם
28.note: See how you translated the similar phrases in Psalm 107:6, 107:13, and 107:19. Alternate translation: [Then they prayed to Yahweh to help them in their trouble and he saved them from it]

The psalmist is using the adjective **distressing** as a noun to mean a certain kind of situation. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [in their distress]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **distresses**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and he rescued them from the distressing things that were happening to them]

29.note: The psalmist is using **raised the storm to calmness** as a common expression of the culture to mean “calmed the storm” or “made the storm stop.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [He made the wind stop blowing]

30.note: The words **they rejoiced** refer to the sailors mentioned in the previous verses who were in distress during the storm. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could clarify this referent. Alternate translation: [Then the people rejoiced]

The words **they subsided** refer to the waves mentioned in the previous verse. If it would be helpful in your language, you could repeat the word “waves” here for clarity. Alternate translation: [because the waves subsided]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **desire**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the harbor where they had desired to arrive]

31.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [for being faithful to his covenant]

The psalmist is using **the sons of man** as a common expression of his culture to mean “people” or “human beings.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [for mankind]

32.note: Here the psalmist is speaking as if the people could physically **exalt** or lift up Yahweh. He means that they should honor and praise him highly. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [May they extol him]

The **seat of the elders** is where the elders gather in a formal setting to make decisions and provide leadership for the community. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and praise him where the elders of the community sit to discuss important issues]

33.note: Here the psalmist is speaking of **land** as if it were a person who could be **thirsty**. He means that the land becomes dry and without water. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [into land that is without water]

34.note: The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [he turns fruitful ground]

Here the psalmist is speaking of **land** as if it were **fruitful ground**. He means land that produces abundant crops. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [productive ground]

Here, **salt land** represents land that cannot produce crops. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [into land that cannot produce crops]

The implication is that God turns fruitful land into salt land because the people living there are wicked. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [because of the wickedness of the dwellers in it]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **wickedness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [because the dwellers in it are so wicked]

The pronoun **it** refers to the fruitful ground that God turns into salt land. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [because of the wickedness of the people who dwell in that land]

35.q: יָשֵׂ֣ם מִ֭דְבָּר לַֽ⁠אֲגַם־מַ֑יִם וְ⁠אֶ֥רֶץ צִ֝יָּ֗ה לְ⁠מֹצָ֥אֵי מָֽיִם
35.note: The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [He turns the wilderness into a pool of water and he turns dry land into springs of water]

35.q: יָשֵׂ֣ם מִ֭דְבָּר לַֽ⁠אֲגַם־מַ֑יִם וְ⁠אֶ֥רֶץ צִ֝יָּ֗ה לְ⁠מֹצָ֥אֵי מָֽיִם
35.note: These two phrases **He turns the wilderness into a pool of water** and **dry land into springs of water** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [He turns the wilderness into a pool of water, yes, dry land into springs of water]

35.q: יָשֵׂ֣ם מִ֭דְבָּר לַֽ⁠אֲגַם־מַ֑יִם וְ⁠אֶ֥רֶץ צִ֝יָּ֗ה לְ⁠מֹצָ֥אֵי מָֽיִם
35.note: The psalmist says this as an overstatement for emphasis. He assumes that readers will know that only parts of the **wilderness** and **dry land** become **water**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [He turns many areas of the wilderness into pools of water and places springs of water throughout the dry land]

36.note: The psalmist is using the adjective **hungry** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [hungry people]

The pronoun **there** refers to the land that Yahweh has transformed from wilderness into a place with pools of water and springs. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [in that land that was dry]

The psalmist is using the possessive form to describe **a city** that is characterized by **dwelling**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [a city to dwell in]

37.note: The implication is that the people are able to settle and farm in the land that God has provided for them. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Then that land is able to produce crops, so they sow fields and plant vineyards there]

The psalmist is using the possessive form **the fruit of the harvest** to describe fruit that is characterized by being harvested. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the crops that grew on the land]

38.note: Here, **and** marks **they become very many** as the goal or purpose of **He blesses them**. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. Alternate translation: [so they become very many]

The psalmist is emphasizing a positive meaning by using a negative word, **not**, together with a mild expression that is the opposite of the intended meaning. If it would be helpful in your language, you could emphasize the positive meaning in a strong way. Alternate translation: [and their cattle become very many]

Here, **and** marks **their cattle do not become few** as the goal or purpose of **He blesses them**. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. Alternate translation: [and so their cattle do not become few]

39.note: Here, **they** could refer to: (1) Yahweh’s people, whom the psalmist describes in verses 36–38. Alternate translation: [Then those people become few and become low] or (2) The enemies of Yahweh’s people. Alternate translation: [Then their enemies become few and become low]

The psalmist is speaking of people as if they could physically **become low**. He means that they become humbled or brought down in status and circumstances. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and become humbled]

The word **from** indicates that what follows is a reason for the result that came before. The people became few and low because of the distress, evil, and sorrow they experienced. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [because of distress of evil and sorrow]

The psalmist is using the possessive form to describe a **distress** that is characterized by **evil and sorrow**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [from distressing evil and sorrow]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **distress**, **evil**, and **sorrow**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [from the evil things that make them distressed and sorrowful]

40.note: Here the psalmist is speaking of **contempt** as if it were a liquid that Yahweh could pour **on the leaders**. The psalmist means that God shows his contempt for these leaders. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [He shows contempt for the leaders]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **contempt**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [He humbles the leaders]

The psalmist is using the possessive form to describe an **empty place** that is characterized by having **no road**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [in a land so empty that there is not even a road]

41.note: Here the psalmist is speaking as if affliction were a physical location from which God **raises up** the needy. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this in a different way. Alternate translation: [But he removes the needy from their affliction]

The psalmist is using the adjective **needy** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [any needy people]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **affliction**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [from what is afflicting them]

The point of this comparison is that just as **a flock** grows and multiplies, so God causes families to increase in number. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and establishes families so that they grow as a healthy flock of sheep grows]

42.note: The psalmist is using the adjective **upright** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [People who do what is right]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [see all of these things]
Here, **wickedness** represents “wicked people.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and every wicked person]

The psalmist is using **shuts its mouth** as a common expression of his culture to mean “can say nothing” or “is silenced.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [can say nothing]

43.note: The psalmist is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [May whoever is wise keep these things]

Here the psalmist is speaking as if Yahweh’s actions that he has been describing were objects that a wise person can **keep**. He means for every wise person to think about these things. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Then may he keep thinking about these things] or [Then may he remember these things]

The psalmist is not referring to a specific **wise** person by saying **may he keep**. He means wise people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Then may they keep]

The pronoun **they** refers to people who are **wise**. These are the same people who are referred to as **he** in the first part of this sentence. Use a way that is natural in your language to indicate that this refers to the same wise people. Alternate translation: [and may all wise people ponder]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the ways that Yahweh is faithful to his covenant with his people]
